title: Sfiha
subtitle: Open Lebanese lamb and tomato flatbreads
excerpt: Sfiha are small open-faced Lebanese flatbreads topped with a spiced lamb and tomato mixture and baked in a hot oven. Similar to lahm bi ajeen but slightly thicker and more bread-like, they are served as a starter or part of a mezze with yoghurt and lemon.
sourceNotes: Claudia Roden, A Book of Middle Eastern Food (1968). Sfiha documented as a characteristic Lebanese and Syrian bakery item, distinct from the thinner lahm bi ajeen. Anissa Helou, Lebanese Cuisine (1994). The dough method and topping described.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze baked and cooled sfiha. Reheat in a hot oven for five minutes.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Prove the dough overnight in the fridge. The topping can be made a day ahead.

content.text: Sfiha are small Lebanese flatbreads with a spiced lamb and tomato topping baked directly on the surface. They are slightly thicker and more bread-like than lahm bi ajeen and closer to a small pizza in texture. The topping is ground finely with onion and tomato and spread over the dough before baking; it caramelises and cooks through in the hot oven. Eat them warm with yoghurt and a squeeze of lemon.

Mix {{yeast-dried}} and {{caster-sugar}} into 260 ml of warm water. Leave five minutes. Combine {{strong-bread-flour}} and {{sea-salt-fine}}, add the yeast mixture and {{olive-oil}}, and knead for eight minutes until smooth. Cover and prove for one hour.

Process {{onion}} and {{tomato}} in a food processor until finely chopped. Drain off excess liquid through a sieve. Add {{lamb-mince}}, {{tomato-puree}}, {{allspice}}, {{cinnamon-ground}}, and {{sea-salt-fine}}. Pulse until well combined but not smooth. Stir in {{pine-nuts}} if using.

Preheat the oven to 230 degrees. Divide the dough into twelve pieces. Roll each into a circle about 12 cm across. Spread a tablespoon of the lamb topping over each one, almost to the edges. Lay on lined baking trays.

Bake for ten to twelve minutes until the dough is cooked through and the edges are golden. The lamb topping should be cooked through and beginning to caramelise. Serve with {{plain-yoghurt}} and {{lemon}} wedges.

items.symptom: The lamb is still pink after twelve minutes
items.fix: Spread the topping no thicker than 5 mm. A thin layer cooks through in the short bake time.

items.cause: Oven not hot enough or dough too thick
items.fix: Preheat fully to 230 degrees and bake on a tray that has been preheated inside the oven. Roll the dough to no more than 4 mm thick.
Drain the processed tomato and onion mixture through a sieve for ten minutes before adding the lamb.

items.symptom: The bread is too bready and thick
items.fix: Each piece should weigh about 55 g. Roll out to 12 cm across: the sfiha should be quite thin relative to its size.

content.text: Sfiha are linked to Baalbek in the Bekaa Valley of Lebanon, where they are sold at roadside stops and eaten on journeys. The Baalbek version is well-spiced and often includes pine nuts in the topping. Across the Levant, sfiha are a common bakery item sold alongside manakish at breakfast. The difference between sfiha and lahm bi ajeen is mainly thickness: sfiha is a thicker, individually-sized piece; lahm bi ajeen is thinner and often rolled up to eat.
